> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-01-game-feel v1.3.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.
> - Missing evidence is UNMEASURED (0 points, not a defect). A test that did not run is NOT_RUN, never PASS. Never invent a measurement; label every worked example synthetic.
> - Game facts and budgets come from your game profile (`pack.profile`). Treat sample numbers as illustrative. Set the frame-time budget separately for each target device in your game profile.
> - An automated gate needs a negative fixture that fails. Receipts carry measured values, never an unconditional PASS.
> Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Game Vibes Director: Getting Started

Measure how quickly a game responds to input and how clearly its camera, sound and visuals communicate each action.

Game Vibes Director is this template's name. Its folder is `01-game-feel` and other templates call it Game Feel (01), because it measures *game feel*: how fast and how clearly the game answers what the player does. It works for any genre and any engine.

If `engine/lens.mjs`, `engine/lens-kit.mjs` or `fixtures/good-pack.json` are not on disk yet, write them byte for byte from the `game-vibes-lens-engine` skill first (Node 18+, no dependencies).

## 1. Onboard one question at a time

Ask one question, wait for the answer, then ask the next. Never stack questions in one message. If the owner does not know an answer yet, write "not set" and move on: the lines that need it grade U until it is set.

1. Which game are we reviewing? Tell me its genre, engine and platforms.
2. Which build should I grade? A build id or commit is enough.
3. Where will the evidence come from: a CI run, a test harness or a manual capture?
4. Which two or three actions do players use most, and what should each one look, sound or feel like when it works? (For example a jump, a tile swap, confirming a move, braking, picking a dialogue choice.)
5. Which controls do you support: mouse and keyboard, touch, gamepad, something else? (`inputDevices`)
6. Which screen sizes should I check, for example desktop and phone? (`viewports`)
7. How fast must an action answer the player on each device, in milliseconds, and how soon after it must the first cue appear? (`inputLatencyP95Ms`, `feedbackCueMaxMs`)
8. Does your game have buffered or held input, such as a jump pressed just before landing or a button held to accelerate? If yes, how much may the repeat rate drift between controls, in percent? (`heldInputMaxDeltaPct`)
9. Does your game have aiming, selecting or steering toward a target? If not, we use the `no-aiming` profile. If yes, does the game help, what aim error is acceptable, and how equal must the help be on touch and gamepad? (`targetingErrorP95Deg`, `assistParityTolerance`)
10. Can anything hurt the player or make them fail from off screen or near its edge? If not, we use the `no-hazards` profile. If yes, how often must it stay visible? (`edgeHazardVisibleMin`, a share from 0 to 1)
11. Does your settings screen offer reduced motion? Which effects does it promise to reduce (shake, flash, zoom), and how much shake, in pixels, is still allowed when it is on? (`reducedMotionShakeMaxPx`)
12. Which style effects are in the game on purpose, so I never mark them down? For example hitstop (a freeze of a few frames on impact), screen shake or platformer moves such as coyote time. This list is your design contract.
13. Is the game online with client prediction, or offline only? If offline only, we use the `offline-only` profile.
14. Which tasks should every control complete, and how many repeat runs per device do you want (at least three)? (`journeyTasks`, `latencyRunIds`)
15. Who reviews the local finding drafts?

Write the answers into the game profile (`pack.profile`), using the profile in `fixtures/good-pack.json` as the shape. Its numbers are synthetic examples, never defaults. Read the profiles you picked back to the owner and, once they approve, set them before scoring, for example `"rubricProfile": ["no-aiming", "offline-only"]`.

### Lines that may not apply to your game

Some lines come from action games. Three of them have an approved profile in `RUBRIC.json`. With the owner's approval, set the profile in `pack.profile.rubricProfile`; that line then reads N/A (not U, not a defect), its partner line takes the pillar's 20 points, and the verdict can reach PASS:

| Profile | Use when the game has | Line that reads N/A | Example genres |
|---|---|---|---|
| `no-aiming` | No aimed, selected or steered input | `control-intent:2` (`targeting` can be left out) | Rhythm, idle and some narrative games |
| `no-hazards` | Nothing that can hurt the player or make them fail from off screen | `camera-comfort:1` (`camera` can be left out) | Calm puzzle, narrative and life sims |
| `offline-only` | No online or predicted simulation path | `parity:1` (still run the offline pair and report it as a note) | Single-player offline games |

These lines have no profile. When your game lacks the feature, leave the group out; the line grades U (0 points, lower coverage) and the verdict stays CONDITIONAL. That is expected for your genre, not a defect. Say so in every report, and never fill a line with made-up values:

| Line | Applies when your game has | If it does not, leave out | Example genres where it often does not apply |
|---|---|---|---|
| `response:2` | Buffered or held input | `heldInput` | Some narrative adventures and turn-based games |
| `readable-feedback:2` | Something that becomes ready again (cooldown, turn, crop, boost) | `readyCue` | Some puzzle games |
| `camera-comfort:2` | Motion effects and a reduced-motion setting | `reducedMotion` | Games with no shake, flash or zoom |

If a game has motion effects but no reduced-motion setting, `camera-comfort:2` stays U; raise it as a note for the owner and for Access, Input and Localization (21).

Before grading a real pack, check that its build and profile match what the owner chose. Record any capture or run that could not happen as NOT_RUN. Use the sample populations (the arrays or case counts each line needs) listed by `node engine/lens.mjs --meta`.

## 2. What you provide

- An evidence pack (JSON) with `status: "VALID"`, a `gitSha` (the source commit), a `liveSha` (the id of the build that was actually played) and a `packId` (all three are required), and an `artifacts` list (the captures and traces the numbers came from). Every metric group names the artifact id it came from.
- Metric groups this engine reads: `latency` (capture), `heldInput` (capture), `hitFeedback` (capture), `readyCue` (trace), `tasks` (capture), `targeting` (capture), `camera` (capture), `reducedMotion` (capture), `simTiming` (trace), `style` (static).
- Profile thresholds in `pack.profile`. A missing threshold makes its line U, never a default.
- Anything you cannot capture yet stays out of the pack. It grades U (UNMEASURED), which is honest and costs no false defect.

## 3. Run the first grade

```
node engine/lens.mjs fixtures/good-pack.json   # worked example, synthetic, not a measurement
node engine/lens.mjs your-pack.json            # your build
node engine/lens.mjs --meta                    # rubric lines, weights and what each reads
node engine/lens.mjs --fixtures fixtures/good-pack.json  # negative and missing-input self-test
```

Read the record: `verdict` (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED or INVALID), `grade` and `coverage`, then each line's `level` and `findings`, then `checks` (growth checks reported beside the grade) and `tickets` (deduplicated candidates).

## 4. Report in plain English

- Lead with the verdict, grade and coverage in one sentence. Say how much of the rubric was measured.
- List U lines as "not measured yet" with the capture that would measure them. Never call them defects. For a line that does not apply to this game, say so instead.
- One local ticket draft per measured finding, with the pack id and artifact ids. Label any synthetic pack as synthetic.
- Findings about a HUD element or a sound also go in a local `feel-findings` file for HUD Designer (09) and Audio Director (13).
- Rubric lines: response:1, response:2, readable-feedback:1, readable-feedback:2, control-intent:1, control-intent:2, camera-comfort:1, camera-comfort:2, parity:1, parity:2.

## 5. Skills in this template

- `game-feel-audit`: Measure how fast and how clearly the game answers the actions players use most, in any genre and any engine, and gather the evidence for each Game Feel rubric line.
- `ship-juice-module`: Add visual, audio or haptic feedback (often called juice) to an action without changing input handling or game timing, behind a switch that is off by default.
- `before-after-feel-proof`: Compare the same player action before and after a feedback change and record both timing and perception.
- `assist-and-forgiveness-check`: Check that aim assist, ledge grabs, snap-to-tile and other input help land where the player meant, the same way on every supported control. Use only when your game has such help.
- `game-vibes-lens-engine`: the engine source and how to run it.

## Blockers to tell the owner about

- Latency and targeting evidence needs captures from the supported input devices; the shipped fixture is synthetic.

Before capture, agree on the case IDs and expected values in `profile.cases` (for example one case per device and run). Run `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` for the required row fields and comparisons. Record one row per approved case under `receipts` (a receipt is that row of measured values), including its id, liveSha and artifact ID. A skipped or stale case leaves its line U. The bundled rows and budgets are synthetic.

description: "Measure how fast and how clearly the game answers the actions players use most, in any genre and any engine, and gather the evidence for each Game Feel rubric line."
---

> **Audit contract v1 (overrides everything below).** Created by @meta_alchemist (https://x.com/meta_alchemist).
> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-01-game-feel v1.3.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.
> - Missing evidence is UNMEASURED (0 points, not a defect). A test that did not run is NOT_RUN, never PASS. Never invent a measurement; label every worked example synthetic.
> - Game facts and budgets come from your game profile (`pack.profile`). Treat sample numbers as illustrative. Set the frame-time budget separately for each target device in your game profile.
> - An automated gate needs a negative fixture that fails. Receipts carry measured values, never an unconditional PASS.
> Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Audit input and feedback

Pick the actions players repeat most. For each one, name the first visible, audible or haptic cue that tells the player the action worked. Examples:

| Genre | Action | First cue |
|---|---|---|
| 2D platformer | Jump | The character leaves the ground; the jump sound starts |
| Mobile puzzle game | Swap two tiles | The tiles start to move; a click or a short vibration |
| Turn-based strategy | Confirm a move | The unit starts to move; a confirm sound |
| Racing game | Brake | The car slows; brake lights and tyre sound |
| Narrative adventure | Pick a dialogue choice | The choice highlights; the next line starts |
| Farming or life sim | Water a crop | The watering animation and splash sound start |
| 3D arena game | Attack | The swing starts; a hit flash and impact sound on contact |

This works in any engine (Unity, Unreal, Godot, a custom engine or a browser build). Log the input time and the cue start on one clock, from an engine trace, a high-speed video or a test harness, and put the numbers in the pack.

## Steps

1. **Delay** (`response:1`, `readable-feedback:1`). Record input time and cue start for each control in `profile.inputDevices`. Say whether the trace stops when the game state changes or when the frame reaches the screen. The second includes display delay and is what players feel. Note whether each cue was visible and audible on each device.
2. **Repeat runs** (`response:1`). Repeat the same action on the same build, camera and device for each run id in `profile.latencyRunIds` (at least three). Compare the p95 (the value 95 percent of samples stay under) with the budget in the profile.
3. **Buffered and held input** (`response:2`). Test a press made just before the game can act on it (a jump pressed just before landing, a move queued during an animation) and a held input (hold to accelerate, charge, drag or fast-forward text). Record them in the `heldInput` group. The name comes from a held fire button, but the group covers any held or repeated input. `onlineMatchesOffline` asks whether the held input behaves the same in the real game mode as in a practice or test scene. If your game has no buffered or held input, leave `heldInput` out and the line stays U.
4. **Ready cues** (`readable-feedback:2`). If something becomes ready again (an ability recharges, a crop is ready to harvest, it is the player's turn, a boost refills), trace that its cue fires exactly once each time. If nothing in your game becomes ready again, leave `readyCue` out.
5. **Task on every control** (`control-intent:1`). Complete each task in `profile.journeyTasks` on each control, including one switch of control in the middle of a task.
6. **Camera framing** (`camera-comfort:1`). Check that anything that can hurt the player or make them fail (an enemy, a hazard, a rival car closing in, a falling piece) stays on screen at each viewport. The rubric calls these "threats". If nothing in your game can hurt or fail the player from off screen, the owner can approve the `no-hazards` profile: `camera-comfort:1` then reads N/A and `camera` can be left out.
7. **Effects never change the game** (`parity:1`). Replay the same inputs and seed with feedback effects on and off, and compare the final game state hash. The rubric compares an offline pair and a predicted pair (client prediction in an online game). If your game is offline only, the predicted pair does not exist: with the owner's approval select the `offline-only` profile, so `parity:1` reads N/A and `parity:2` takes the pillar's points. Report the offline result as a note.
8. **Reduced motion** (`camera-comfort:2`). List the motion reductions your settings promise (shake, flash, zoom). Turn the setting on, replay the same camera path and confirm each one is applied.
9. **Prove the check can fail.** In a test copy, remove one feedback cue and confirm that your evidence check reports it missing. Keep both captures and the build id.

When a finding is about a HUD element or a sound, save it in a local `feel-findings` file (for example `.grokbot-team/artifacts/feel-findings/<pack id>.json`) for HUD Designer (09) or Audio Director (13): one entry per action with the action, device, measured delay, the missing or late cue, the pack id and the capture ids.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>`.

# Implement action feedback

"Juice" is the extra feedback that makes an action feel good: a flash, a sound, a small camera move, a vibration. This skill adds it without changing what the game does.

## 1. Hook feedback to a game event

Send an existing gameplay event to a presentation handler. Keep the action, its time and its strength in the event data. Examples:

| Genre | Event | Feedback |
|---|---|---|
| 2D platformer | Landing | A dust puff and a landing thud, stronger after a long fall |
| Mobile puzzle game | A piece snaps into place | A highlight and a short vibration |
| Turn-based strategy | A unit finishes its move | A small settle animation and a footstep sound |
| Racing game | Hitting a wall | A short camera shake and a scrape sound |
| Narrative adventure | A new clue is found | A soft glow on the item and a chime |
| Farming or life sim | Harvest | Crops pop into the basket with a pluck sound |
| 3D arena game | A hit lands | Hitstop (a freeze of a few frames on impact), a flash and an impact sound |

Hitstop, shake and similar effects are style choices. Add them only when the owner's design contract (their written list of intended effects) includes them.

## 2. Keep game logic and presentation apart

Run the game simulation and the presentation on separate clocks: effects read the game state and never write to it. Drive fades from elapsed time so they look the same at any frame rate. Apply camera offsets to the rendered camera after aiming, picking or targeting has been computed, so a shake never moves where the player's input lands. Expose duration, strength and a reduced-motion option in the game's settings. Cap simultaneous effects with measured CPU, GPU and audio budgets.

For a camera shake that decays the same way at any frame rate, scale its strength each frame by `exp(-decayPerSecond * elapsedSeconds)`. In JavaScript: `intensity *= Math.exp(-decayPerSecond * elapsedSeconds)`. Sample the result only when rendering, and keep the unshaken camera for input and simulation.

## 3. Prove it changed nothing else

Capture a replay twice with the same input and seed, with the feedback on and off. Check that the game state matches, that the cue appears at the intended time, and that the reduced-motion run removes or softens the promised effects. Measure frame time on a target device at the busiest moment of effects.

The new feedback sits behind a switch that is off by default. Test the switch missing, invalid and explicitly off: each case must keep the original input and timing. Then test the effects switched on, with reduced motion on, and keep both captures.

Use typed settings in the presentation code. A request flag can only turn on an effect the owner has approved:

```js
function effectEnabled(ownerOptIn, requestFlag) {
  return ownerOptIn === true && requestFlag === true;
}
```

## 4. Hand on what other templates need

If the feedback adds or changes a sound, note the event name and its priority for Audio Director (13). If it adds or changes a HUD element, note it for HUD Designer (09). Put both in the local `feel-findings` file with the pack id and capture ids.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>`.

Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Capture a comparable pair

A before and after comparison is only fair when everything except the feedback change stays the same. Fix the build, input sequence, device, camera and scenario. Either use an effects switch on one build, or record the revision of each build. Capture the input, the moment the action takes effect and the first player-facing cue on one clock.

Examples of a fair pair:

- **2D platformer:** the same recorded jump sequence on the same level, before and after a new landing sound.
- **Mobile puzzle game:** the same seeded board and the same swaps, before and after a new snap vibration.
- **Racing game:** the same replayed lap on the same car and track, before and after a new impact shake.
- **Narrative adventure:** the same dialogue path from the same save, before and after a new choice highlight.

| Evidence | What to record |
|---|---|
| Responsiveness | Input-to-cue times, the sample count and the device |
| Readability | Matched clips at playback size and what the reviewer saw |
| Gameplay parity | Final state or replay hash for the same inputs |
| Performance | Frame-time distribution and the peak number of effects at once |
| Accessibility | The same sequence with the game's reduced-motion or sound alternatives on |

Keep the raw ids of both clips. In a test copy, delay one cue on purpose and confirm that the timing comparison shows the change.

## Receipt rows this skill fills

A receipt is one row per approved test case with the measured values (see `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` for the fields).

- `pairedTiming` (`parity:1`): one row per replay pair. Use the replay id as the run key on both sides, keep both trace files, and compare tick counts before comparing the game state hashes.
- `readyEmissions` (`readable-feedback:2`): one row per traced ready event, naming the code that emitted the cue and its source line in the measured build.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>`.

# Check assists and input forgiveness

An *assist* is help the game adds to the player's input: aim assist, a ledge grab, a tap that snaps to the nearest tile, steering help. *Forgiveness* is a small allowance that lets a nearly correct input still count, such as a jump pressed a few frames after running off a ledge (often called coyote time) or a press stored just before landing (a jump buffer). Both should do what the player meant and behave the same on every supported control.

Skip this skill if your game has no assists and no forgiveness windows. Never add one just to fill a rubric line.

## 1. List what your game does

Write each assist or window into the game profile notes with its trigger, its limit (time, distance or angle) and the controls it applies to. Examples:

| Genre | Assist or forgiveness to check | "Landed as intended" means |
|---|---|---|
| 2D platformer | Coyote time, jump buffer, ledge grab | The jump or grab happens inside the window and never outside it |
| 3D arena game | Aim assist on pad and touch | The attack lands on the intended target, with the same assist strength on each control |
| Mobile puzzle game | A drag that snaps to a tile | The piece lands on the tile the player touched, never a neighbour |
| Racing game | Steering or braking assist | The car follows the line the player steered, at the assist level the setting promises |
| Turn-based strategy | Cursor snapping to units or tiles | The selected unit or tile is the one under the cursor or finger |
| Narrative adventure | Auto-highlight of the nearest object | The highlighted object is the one the player faces or touches |

## 2. Replay cases at the edges

For each assist or window, replay inputs just inside and just outside its limit on each supported control. Add one case where the target is out of reach or hidden and record the expected refusal. Keep one capture at gameplay size for every case.

If your game has height differences, test targets above, below and next to an obstruction as seen by the gameplay camera. In a 2D game, compare the input point with the selected or landing point on the screen.

## 3. Record the evidence

- **Directional aiming** (shooting, throwing, a golf or pool shot, a slingshot puzzle): record one p95 aim error in degrees per control in `targeting.errorDegP95` (p95 is the value 95 percent of samples stay under), whether the assist is written down for players in `targeting.assistDocumented`, and the assist strength on touch and pad in `targeting.touchAssist` and `targeting.padAssist`. These feed `control-intent:2`.
- **No aimed, selected or steered input:** the owner can approve the `no-aiming` profile before scoring (`"rubricProfile": ["no-aiming"]` in the game profile). `control-intent:2` then reads N/A, not U and not a defect, `control-intent:1` takes the pillar's 20 points, and the `targeting` group can be left out. Without that approval, leave `targeting` out and the line stays U. Never fill it with made-up values.
- **Jump buffers and held input** feed `response:2`; see `game-feel-audit`.
- Window and snapping results that have no metric field go in the report as notes and local ticket drafts, never as invented metric values.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>`.

memory.content: AUDIT CONTRACT V1: score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-01-game-feel v1.3.0), 100 points, 5 pillars of 20, levels 0 to 4, pass at level 3. Grade with `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` and report the grade with coverage and verdict (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED, INVALID). UNMEASURED earns 0 and is never a defect; N/A is excluded from averages. Review focus for this template: Measure input-to-feedback delay for a representative action, capture legibility on supported controls and verify the reduced-motion option against the design contract.

ENGINE: the lens engine is embedded in the game-vibes-lens-engine skill. Write both files byte for byte before the first run. Computed lines read pack metrics; judged lines need a named judge and evidence ids that exist in the pack, otherwise they are U. Computed lines trust pack.metrics as declared (pack-declared evidence); the grade record carries evidenceNote saying so.

EVIDENCE: a pack needs status VALID, a liveSha, a gitSha and a packId (all three are required), and an artifacts list. Metric groups read: latency, heldInput, hitFeedback, readyCue, tasks, aim, camera, reducedMotion, simTiming, style. Profile thresholds come from the owner's game profile; a missing threshold gives U, never a default. Check the sample populations listed by the engine in --meta. Empty evidence earns U. Field names come from an action game but fit any genre: heldInput is any buffered or held input, hitFeedback is the chosen action's feedback, readyCue is any ready-again cue, camera threats are anything that can hurt the player or make them fail.

ONBOARDING: ask one question at a time and wait for each answer. Settle early, in plain questions: how fast each action must answer on each device and how soon its first cue must appear; if players aim, the acceptable aim error and how equal aim help must be across controls; which style effects (hitstop, a freeze of a few frames on impact; screen shake; platformer moves such as coyote time) are in the game on purpose, written down as the design contract; whether the game has aiming, selecting or steering toward a target (if not, the no-aiming profile), anything that can hurt the player from off screen (if not, no-hazards) and an online predicted mode (if not, offline-only), each approved by the owner before scoring.

HOUSE RULES: use the frame-time and response targets for each supported device from the game profile. No en or em dashes. Write the game's full name. Credit @meta_alchemist. Label every worked example synthetic and never invent a measurement.

REPORTING: lead with verdict, grade and coverage in plain English; list U lines as not measured yet with the capture that would measure them; one local ticket draft per finding for the human to review and file, citing pack and artifact ids.

BLOCKERS: Latency and aim evidence needs captures from each supported control; the shipped fixture is synthetic. NOT APPLICABLE: approved profiles no-aiming (control-intent:2), no-hazards (camera-comfort:1) and offline-only (parity:1). The owner approves them before scoring and sets rubricProfile in the game profile; the line reads N/A, its partner line takes the pillar's 20 points, the verdict can reach PASS, and the report names the profiles. No held input (response:2), no ready-again cue (readable-feedback:2) or no motion effects (camera-comfort:2) has no profile: leave that group out, the line grades U, the verdict stays CONDITIONAL and the report says the line does not apply. Never fill a line with made-up values.
